items.content:
Your KPI Is Not the Problem. It Is the Symptom.
Many organizations spend hours reviewing KPIs.
Productivity is down.
Rejections are up.
Breakdowns have increased.
Customer complaints are rising.
The discussion often focuses on the numbers.
But KPIs are not the problem.
They are simply indicators that a problem exists somewhere in the system.
A declining OEE is not the issue.
The issue may be poor maintenance practices.
A rising rejection rate is not the issue.
The issue may be process variation, inadequate training, or unclear standards.
A late delivery is not the issue.
The issue may be poor planning, bottlenecks, or communication gaps.
When leaders focus only on improving the KPI, they often treat symptoms.
When leaders focus on understanding the system, they eliminate the causes.
The best organizations do not manage numbers.
They manage processes.
Because when the process improves, the numbers follow.
What is your experience?
Have you seen teams focus more on the KPI than the system driving it?

🚨 Your foundry's biggest cost may not be raw material, labour, or energy. It may be the waste you no longer notice.
Everyone talks about scrap.
Almost nobody talks about the losses that are silently destroying profitability every single day.
The biggest problem in most foundries isn't scrap.
It's hidden losses.
Think about it.
When a casting gets rejected, the loss isn't limited to the value of the scrap metal.
The real cost includes:
• Additional melting and re-melting
• Excess energy consumption
• Additional labour hours
• Machine downtime
• Production schedule disruption
• Delayed deliveries
• Customer dissatisfaction
And scrap is only one part of the story.
What about:
❓ Waiting time between processes?
❓ Frequent furnace stoppages?
❓ Excess inventory lying on the shop floor?
❓ Rework that has become "normal"?
❓ Inefficient material movement?
❓ Capacity lost due to poor planning?
These losses rarely appear on a Profit & Loss statement.
Yet they quietly erode margins month after month.
Many foundries invest heavily in new machines, automation, and capacity expansion.
But sustainable profitability often comes from a different source:
Identifying, measuring, and eliminating hidden losses through systematic Continuous Improvement.
The foundries that will lead the next decade will not necessarily be the largest.
They will be the ones that relentlessly improve Quality, Productivity, Delivery, Cost, and Safety.

items.content:
A 15-minute daily machine jam does not show up on your monthly P&L. But it is quietly stealing ₹25 Lakhs from your bottom line every year.
Walk across any shop floor, and you will see operators dealing with "minor" issues. A sensor trips, a conveyor jams, or a feeder needs manual adjustment.
Because it only takes a few minutes to clear, it never gets logged as downtime. The operator just deals with it. This normalization of micro-stoppages is a silent EBITDA killer.
Let's do the math on a single bottleneck machine: A 15-minute stoppage per shift. Across 3 shifts, that is 45 minutes of lost production daily. Over 300 working days, you have lost 225 hours of pure manufacturing capacity.
If that line generates ₹10,000 of product per hour, that "minor annoyance" is costing you over ₹22 Lakhs in lost revenue, plus the cost of wasted operator wages and utilities.
You cannot scale profitability if your baseline process is bleeding time.
Lean Six Sigma stops treating these jams as operator tasks and treats them as engineering failures. By applying root-cause analysis and implementing robust poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), you eliminate the stoppage permanently.
You do not need to buy a faster machine to increase your revenue. You just need to stop the one you have from stopping.
Are you ready to fix the root cause and get that ₹25 Lakhs back?

The Cost of a Problem Is Not When It Happens. It's When We Accept It.

A quality defect is a problem.

Your 5% defect rate isn't a quality control issue. It is a ₹2 Crore hole in your annual EBITDA.
Most plant directors accept a baseline of scrap, rework, and equipment downtime as the standard cost of doing business. This is a critical strategic error.
When you isolate shop-floor data from boardroom financials, you blind yourself to the actual cash bleed.
Let’s look at the real math. A defective unit does not just cost you raw materials.
It burns energy, machine time, and operator wages.
It demands secondary labor for inspection, sorting, and rework.
Most dangerously, it traps capital that should be circulating in your cash flow.
In a plant doing ₹50 Crores in revenue, an "acceptable" 5% defect rate easily scales into the Crores in lost profit margins.
Lean Six Sigma is not a theoretical exercise meant to keep your quality department busy. It is a rigorous, mathematical business strategy designed to protect your margins and scale your operations.
By applying statistical process control and eliminating root-cause variations, you do not just improve a metric on a clipboard. You permanently seal the leaks in your cash flow and release trapped capital back into your business.
You cannot scale a plant's profitability if the operational foundation is leaking cash.

items.content:
Most business owners chase the big win.
The new hire. The new product. The rebrand. The big strategy day.
But the businesses that quietly outgrow everyone else? They're focused on something much smaller.
1%.
Improve by just 1% every single day, and in a year you'll be 37× better than you are today. That's not a motivational poster — that's compound improvement, and it works the same way compound interest does.
Dave Brailsford used it to turn British Cycling from also-rans into Olympic champions. He didn't look for one big breakthrough. He looked for a 1% improvement in everything — tyres, pillows, hand-washing technique, nutrition timing. Individually, none of it mattered. Together, they won 60% of the gold medals at Beijing 2008.
Your SME works the same way.
Shorten one meeting by 5 minutes. Add one follow-up question to your next client call. Remove one unnecessary approval step. Reply to enquiries 30 minutes faster.
None of those feel significant. That's exactly the point.
The 1% rule has only one enemy — inconsistency. Improving for 3 days and stopping for 4 doesn't compound. It stalls. So swipe through this carousel for the simple 3-question daily habit that keeps the 1% going — every single day.

Most SME owners open their inbox before they've had a chance to think.
By 9am they're already firefighting. By 5pm they're exhausted — and roughly where they started. The business runs them. Not the other way around.
One operations manager I know started doing something different. Before opening a single email, he spent 15 minutes with his team on one question:
"What's ONE thing we could do better today than we did yesterday?"
That question — asked every morning, consistently — became the engine behind everything that changed in his business.
His team was a 14-person engineering services firm. Within 4 weeks of starting this routine, they had recovered ₹40,000 a month from a billing error pattern no one had ever stopped to notice. Total investment: 15 minutes a day. Four people. Twenty working days.
Week 1 — they found 3 recurring delays in their job handover process. Week 2 — they standardised the checklist. Delays dropped by half. Week 3 — they spotted the billing error pattern. Week 4 — fixed. Recovered. Ongoing.
No consultant. No new software. No budget. Just one question, asked every morning before the noise started.
The habit doesn't require a meeting room or a strategy deck. It requires one question, one answer, and one small action — written down where everyone can see it.

document.title: You Dont need a big a big budget to start Kaizen

items.content:
Most SME owners have done this at least once.
Big strategy day. New consultant. New software. New 90-day plan. Everyone leaves the room feeling energised.
Three months later — half the team has reverted to the old way of doing things, the consultant's invoice has been paid, and the problem is still there.
This is the Big Bang approach. And research suggests it fails around 70% of the time in small businesses — not because the ideas are bad, but because the method is wrong for how SMEs actually work.
Kaizen is the opposite.
Instead of one massive change, it asks for one small improvement. Every day. The team suggests it. The cost is near zero. You see results in 2–3 weeks. And because the change is small enough to absorb, it actually sticks.
One SME spent £18,000 on a CRM rollout that the team quietly abandoned within months. Another solved the same underlying problem — slow sales follow-ups — by asking their team one question and building a single email template in an afternoon. Follow-up rate up 40%. Cost: zero.
Same problem. Completely different approaches. Completely different outcomes.

items.content: ✅ Procurement vs. Sourcing vs. Purchasing

author.name: Sourcing & Procurement Group
author.info: Onesphore RAKOTOMALALA • 3rd+

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 months ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

repost.content:
Procurement, Sourcing, Purchasing. What is the difference?

Many still mix up these terms, yet each covers a distinct aspect of the supply chain:

✦ Procurement covers the full process.
 ⤷ It creates value across the entire lifecycle.

✦ Sourcing focuses on supplier selection.
 ⤷ It weighs cost, quality, and long-term alignment.

✦ Purchasing handles transactions.
 ⤷ It meets immediate operational needs.

Simply put:
Procurement = Sourcing + Purchasing ➝ combined to support sustainable and cost-effective operations.
